🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -0.08% (intraday, 7-year +1bp). At trading day 20 (last close) it was -0.95% against a five-campaign average of -1.12% at the same point — 1994-95, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.42%. The 10-year is +4bp since the hike vs a +19bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 3 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 732bp against a five-year average of 411bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +47bp and BB +39bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.31 → 0.57 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+4bp).

The biggest story this morning is a broad, global bond rally. The US 10Y is down 13.16 bp to 5.0538%, the 30Y is down 13.07 bp to 5.3924% and the 2Y is down 6.98 bp to 4.7277%. Bunds (-11 bp to 3.356%), JGBs (-10.2 bp to 2.900%) and Gilts (-12 bp to 5.304%) are rallying with them, and 10Y note futures are up 0.796875 to 105.671875. The bond bid follows a hard risk-off session led by tech. In the prior session the Nasdaq fell 1.880% (-511.51 to 26,692.87), the Russell 2000 fell 1.934%, the S&P 500 fell 1.108% to 7,718.94, and the Dow lost only 0.094%. The Nikkei then fell 4.898% (-3,318.34 to 64,425.95). US Info Tech dropped 2.62% on the day while Health Care (+2.44%) and Staples (+2.38%) rallied, a clear defensive rotation. Futures show the same split: NQ is -1.194% but Dow futures are +0.499%, with ES -0.251%. The dollar is softer (DXY -0.444 to 102.109) and gold is up 1.17% to 4,153.47, both consistent with a flight to safety rather than a growth scare. Brent is down 1.91 to 104.15 even as Gulf shipping attacks escalate. Under the surface, junk credit is the warning light. The Caa–B spread gap is at 732 bp, the 100th percentile of the past five years and the widest since 2020-04-24. It has widened 216 bp in three months, and the outright Caa OAS is 1,045 bp, up 256 bp over the same period. Is the CCC stress spreading up the ladder? Partly. Single-B OAS widened 47 bp in a month to 313 bp and Ba widened 39 bp to 196 bp, so the outright levels are moving. But the B–Ba gap is 117 bp, below its 5y average of about 128.8 bp, and IG is only +4 bp in a month at 83 bp. The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes has risen to 0.574 from 0.357 a month ago, still below its 5y median of 0.699. So the CCC rot is starting to pull B and BB wider in absolute terms, but it has not yet broken the quality ladder in relative terms or reached IG. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. Overall sentiment is defensive but orderly: VIX is 17.45 (+0.58), and IG and HY index OAS are still at the 8th and 22nd historical percentiles.

“When the 10-year falls 13 bp, the Nikkei drops almost 5% and CCCs are at a five-year wide all on the same morning, it's time to own quality and let someone else buy the tech dip.”

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 479.11 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD sits at 479.11 cents/gal, at the 99.8th percentile with a z-score of 3.24. The crack spread is at 106.0662 $/bbl (z 5.77), so the refining margin is even more stretched than the outright price. The curve is in steep backwardation: the front month is 479.11, the 12th month is 372.5 and the 36th month is 285.18. That points to a squeeze in prompt supply rather than a structural repricing of diesel. Historically, extremes this concentrated in the front month have tended to mean-revert, but with backwardation this steep, short positions are exposed to violent squeezes until prompt tightness eases.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.91 vol points (74th percentile of the 43 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 99.1 (71th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 98bp (steeper by 22bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Cup test

COMPONENTLEVELDATE

Right rim5.30%2026-10-05

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (110bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 14 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 58/100 — Sticky, but not re-accelerating at the core. Underlying measures sit in the mid-2s to around 3%: Core PCE 3.00759%, Median CPI 2.61045%, Trimmed-Mean CPI 2.66487%, Median PCE 2.56715%, Trimmed-Mean PCE 2.19% and Core Sticky CPI 2.7765%. Most are falling or flat (computed direction), and the computed Core-Trend sub-score is only moderately elevated. The pressure is in the flexible, energy-linked basket: Flexible CPI is 6.1232% and rising (computed). Breadth is two-sided: per the Dallas Fed distribution, 13.2% of the PCE basket is inflating above 10% and 15.7% at 5–10%, while 25.8% is falling. That leaves the Fed facing a supply-shock problem layered on a sticky but drifting core, which argues for vigilance rather than aggressive further tightening.

Rich, but not March 2000, and the evidence is mixed across dimensions. On Equity Froth the computed gauges are far from the dot-com peak: Nasdaq trailing P/E is 41.99x against 175x at the peak (17% of the way there), the price stretch versus the 200DMA is 7.2% against 50% (14%), and semis are the frothiest at a 40.07x SOX P/E (50% of the 60x peak). On Late-cycle Catalyst, credit is tighter than in 2000: IG spread tightness computes at 130% and Baa–10Y at 154% of the 2000 condition. On Bear-Market Signposts, VIX complacency (181%) and loose financial conditions (NFCI, 154%) exceed 2000 levels. Sentiment does not: AAII is at 42%, consumer confidence at 17% and margin-debt growth at 46%. In aggregate, the valuation backdrop (CAPE about 41.6x, Buffett indicator about 236%, both near records) rhymes with 2000. Price action, sentiment and the macro regime do not, so this looks more like a late-stage valuation problem than a terminal mania.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (42x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The computed overlay puts the current cycle, anchored at the Oct-2022 low, at month 48 with a value of 242.9. The 1994-anchored dot-com path was at 268.4 at the same point and peaked at month 69. On that analogy the current cycle is tracking slightly behind the dot-com run, with roughly 21 months to go before the analog peak, if the analogy holds at all. The valuation marker sits at 24% (computed), versus a trailing Nasdaq P/E of 41.99x today and 175x in 2000, and the dot-com bust that followed took the Nasdaq down 78% over 31 months. Analyst-estimate inputs (not computed): Shiller CAPE about 41.6x per a daily Multpl-based estimate for 8 October 2026, close to the December-1999 monthly peak of 44.19. The Buffett indicator is about 236–237%. Top-10 S&P concentration is about 35% per a June-2026 report, so that figure is stale and should be treated as approximate. IPO froth (about 30) and long-term EPS-growth expectations (about 70) are judgment calls, not sourced figures: the IPO pipeline is active (India's record Jio deal) but US issuance this week looks thin, and Street long-term growth assumptions remain elevated because of AI capex. Today's selloff, Nasdaq -1.88% and Nikkei -4.9% with rotation into defensives, is the kind of leadership crack that tends to appear before froth peaks rather than after. With tight credit spreads, low VIX and loose NFCI all past their 2000 analogs, the bigger risk is complacency in credit and volatility pricing, not equity euphoria.

⚔️Iran War

The conflict is escalating at sea while diplomacy stalls. A maritime monitor cited by CBS says ships in the Strait of Hormuz still face 'indiscriminate attacks' even with tracking switched off. It has recorded 23 attacks since the start of October, almost double the war's monthly average. Fox News reports 10 ship attacks so far this week, including a container ship sunk by an unknown projectile, and an attack on Saudi Aramco's headquarters that sent oil prices sharply higher on Wednesday. NBC reports a missile attack on Riyadh's airport that killed 13 people. On diplomacy, CBS reports that Iran's Supreme National Security Council head called the latest US response 'insufficient', with talks to end the war and fully reopen Hormuz stalled. Fox describes Trump as holding off on new Hormuz strikes ahead of the midterms. Timelines of the earlier ceasefire differ across sources: iranwarlive says the Islamabad Memorandum collapsed on July 7–8 and expired on August 17, while Dawn gives a different sequence. Market read: Brent is down 1.91 to 104.15 this morning even as attacks accelerate. That suggests the market already prices a supply premium, but the trend in incidents argues the risk is skewed to the upside for oil.

Sources: CBS News – Iran War Updates: Ships in Strait of Hormuz still face 'indiscriminate attacks' · CBS News – Iran calls U.S. response 'insufficient' amid stalled talks · Fox News – Oil price hikes, Saudi-Houthi strikes carry on amid Trump's midterm pause (Oct 14) · NBC News – Iran War: Latest News · Iran War Live tracker · Dawn – Live Updates: Iran-Israel war

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Hold at 3.75%–4.00% at the Oct 27–28 FOMC is the base case (analyst inference). Market-implied odds of an October hike were cited at about 16–18% as of Oct 9, and Goldman reportedly expected the Fed to skip October given its proximity to the midterms. This morning's 6.98 bp drop in the 2Y to 4.7277% leans the same way.

~1 YEAR

Inference, flagged: Warsh framed the September hike as removing 'a dose of accommodation', implying he does not see policy as restrictive yet. Sixteen of 19 FOMC participants expected at least one more hike in 2026. Over about a year, the most likely path is one more 25 bp hike (December more likely than October), followed by an extended hold. The alternative is a pivot to holding if junk-credit stress and the oil shock slow growth. Warsh's declared reluctance to give forward guidance means policy will be more data-reactive and less telegraphed than under his predecessors. That point is drawn from his refusal to give a rate forecast at the September press conference; his broader balance-sheet views were not verified in this run's searches.

At the September 16 FOMC the Fed hiked 25 bp to 3.75%–4.00% in a 12-0 vote, its first hike since 2023. Warsh said inflation is 'still too high' and declined to give a forecast or dot. The move defied Trump's calls for cuts, and Warsh has publicly pushed back on the President's rate critiques. Several Fed officials took a hawkish tone heading into October, per Chase's survey of Fed speakers. Today's macro mix gives a 'hold and watch' Fed something to work with: core inflation sticky around 3% (Core PCE 3.00759%), flexible and energy prices running hot, labor still solid (claims 199k, unemployment 4.2%), and the start of credit stress in the CCC tail. Where this goes beyond the cited sources, it is inference.
